image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - A **faceted heatmap / tiled time-series chart** with one row per product category and one tile per time period, colored by percent change from 12 months prior.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples by category**: each product category appears in its own horizontal row.
   - **Grid of repeated tiles over time**: tiles are arranged sequentially across years.
   - **Color encoding** shows magnitude and direction of change (blue to red diverging scale).
   - No stacking is used.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (months across 2019–2021) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Product category (Televisions; Gasoline (all types); Used cars and trucks; Eyeglasses and eye care; Chicken; Sports equipment; Home furniture) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting by row / position on y-axis |
| Change from 12 months prior (%) | Quantitative | Color/hue of tiles (diverging blue–red scale) |
| Year (2019, 2020, 2021) | Temporal | Group labels/section labels above the x-axis |

comments.raw_comment:
Title: What comes down must go up (at least in terms of prices)


In my opinion this graph is misleading. By just glancing at this graph, one would think that the price of gas and vehicles has gotten higher every month. But because the graph is compared to the previous years prices, this is untrue. While it is true that prices for these things have gone up, because they were so low at the same time the previous year, the are about the same that they were before the pandemic started. This trend is consistent more or less throughout the graph. Also, because the prices are not compared to the previous months, they are not going up month to month, they are only higher compared to last years prices. Also most of these products have reasons other than inflation for their increase in price e.g. televisions because of the perceived shortage of computer chips, gasoline because of the increase in oil prices, and used vehicles because of the shortage of chips to make new vehicle, limiting the supply of new vehicles, thus creating a higher demand for used vehicles. I wounded why the graph is comparing prices from the previous year and not the previous month. I also wonder why these specific products were chosen to be in the graph.

Title: Stock Market Rush

I noticed that this graph is showing the inflation of prices for various products including televisions, sports equipment, and eyeglasses. The main thing that I noticed with this graph is that past 2021 the prices of most of these products have increased greatly after in most cases a steady decline or just a small amount of increase occurring each month. What I've also noticed is that the prices of televisions steadily decreased each month (20%) into mid-2020 and then from there began to increase into now, with a 10% increase starting into 2021. Another thing that is prominent in this graph is that the prices of gasoline have been unsteady going up and down over the years and recently began to rise with an over 20% increase. I think that this is due to the changes in fossil fuel digging over the years and that more recently the supply has become scarce causing the prices to rise.  This is similar to the recent increase in the price of used cars as the computer chips that are needed to make them run have become difficult to find and produce. I wonder if the prices will continue to increase for both these items and others over time or if after a while of increasing they will begin to decrease at some point. I also wonder if since materials are becoming scarce for a lot of things if companies will stop production or if they will continue to produce them but at a large price. And if this were to continue happening, would people start to make more money?

A1:Inflation of prices seems to be widespread throughout these products and services. Some products are observing severe price inflation like gas and used cars. A lot of recent trends can likely be explained by the Coronavirus pandemic because under the pandemic people were not buying as many products and services because of the stay-at-home order and economic crisis. This is shown especially with the price of gasoline, as it experienced a large amount of deflation in 2020, as people weren’t driving as much to go places. But in 2021, as the mask mandate has lifted, places are reopening, and people are returning to their job sites the demand for gasoline is much greater than in 2020. The same explanation can be used for sports equipment, as the pandemic restricted and decreased the amount of sports activity.
A2:What is making television begin to go up in price again? What is responsible for the recent inflation in home furniture? What part of the pandemic made chicken’s price inflate in 2020? How are lower-income people ever going to be able to afford a car if both used car and truck prices and gas prices are rapidly inflating? 
A3:These are all products we consume, and in some cases rely on. The affordability of products directly affects the living conditions of our residents and their economic situation. If prices continue to inflate for most products it’ll be harder for people to live.
A4:Everything is expensive now? Why is inflation so prevalent in our recovering world?

I notice that recently, all of the prices of the items included in the graph are rising in relation to 12 months ago, especially gasoline, which has risen an estimated 20% since last year.

comments.raw_comment: This graph shows the inflation and deflation rates of items from 2019-2021. Something that I notice is that the biggest increase in inflation was with gasoline. In my community, the gas prices have gone up tremendously in the past 6 months. I wonder what this is exactly from. I can infer that COVID has had a big impact on these rates. Used cars and trucks have also been impacted tremendously by inflation. The automobile industry is getting hit very hard, most likely because of the reopening up of the country. I also noticed that the price of home furniture is starting to go up. The shipping wait for items is so long because everything is so backed up. Most people buy their home furniture off of websites and so the prices are going up because of how long it takes to ship things now. Sports were at a stop at one point because of COVID and now that schools and towns are starting up sports again, inflation has increased. A big question that I have is when these inflation rates are going to go down. COVID has had such a big effect on the economy and inflation and so I wonder if in the future the rates will go down or maybe go back up. This affects my community because the gas rates in my town are very high and, just like the rest of the world, the shipping times for so many online items is so long. A catchy headline is "The U.S. is Inflating".

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, I notice how out of the seven featured product genres listed on the left side of the graph, televisions are the item that's price decreased the longest amount of time over the last three years. I also notice how gasoline (all types) and used cars and trucks' prices increased the most over the four other products, especially in 2021. However, gasoline prices increased more suddenly than used cars and trucks in 2021. I wonder why gasoline prices decreased exponentially in 2020, and then suddenly increased the same amount in 2021. I believe this graph is showing seven different product groups and a timeline of their inflation and/or deflation over the last three years. My guess for the reason behind the gasoline prices deflation and inflation in 2020 and 2021 is because of COVID-19 regulations lessening in 2021 since 2020's nationwide quarantine. Also, since the last election, the average price per gallon of regular gasoline in the U.S. has increased by 75 cents. This graph relates to me and my community because it affects my families' average spending on these everyday items which affects our financial state. We also have more than one car, so gasoline prices affect our lives every time we have to fill our gas tanks again. Finally, a headline that summarizes this graph is "America's Everyday Item Prices and COVID-19's effect."

Welcome to Wednesday's line moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs show the changes in a sample of consumer product prices, year-to-year (see the Release for an explanation).   

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?" and  "What do you wonder?"  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, October 22 with moderation on Wednesday, October 27.  The topic:  election redistricting based on the 2020 U.S. Census.  Keep noticing and wondering!

comments.raw_comment:
U.S. economy still positive for Covid19.
The pandemic has hit the world economy hard. Even the economically most prosperous countries are still not recovering, and this is what we are currently seeing with inflation in the United States. The graph shows how prices have skyrocketed by 10% to 20% in the cost of gasoline, home furniture, some foods such as chicken, sports equipment, and new and used vehicles. The shortage of these products is the leading cause of the price increase due to global supply chains and the lack of people to enter the workforce. 
This economic phenomenon can bring significant consequences for the world economy. The planet continues to show us how vulnerable our economic systems are. Therefore, We should take advantage of this opportunity and this financial crisis to seek alternative solutions that can allow us to move forward.
In the case of the increase in the price of vehicles and gasoline, many governments could be motivating their citizens to purchase electric cars, whose maintenance is much cheaper and environmentally friendly. Moreover, the oil industry should be reduced or ended soon for the benefit of all.
Another essential aspect that we as citizens can consider is to promote local purchasing. Many local food producers, farmer markets, and even the local furniture industry need support. Opting for these and not for imported products instead would be contributing to lessening the impact of the economic crisis.

I observe the price fluctuation of items (all with different benefits to life) over the past year. I imagine these items were the ones chosen to compared because each one (with the exception of Gasoline and Used cars and trucks because they both relate to the automotive industry) adds to the diverse influx of prices; it shows this was not just inflation in one industry but widely effecting.  From examining the trends, I concluded that Eyeglasses and eye care was the sole data type that did not increase in price over the past year.

Why were Eyeglasses and eye care unaffected by this wide-scale, hybrid, inflation? I wonder why there has been such serious inflation over the past 12 months? Has the supply chain collapse had an impact on the recent lack of goods or high expenses?

My community is greatly affected by these price increases because even though the costs of goods are increasing, income is not. We are now forced to survive on what we have been producing (income) but account for the rise in prices of food, gasoline, furniture, etc. which is very challenging. It is a difficult world we live in and inflation is just one of those imperfections which make life resemble a rollercoaster. 

Understanding the graph represents the alteration of prices over the years, an appropriate title for this graph would be:
The Price's Flight

comments.raw_comment:
Headline: "The Dramatic Inflation of Everyday Items: How will it change the future?"

What do you notice?
Prices of common items are going up drastically. For example, televisions, which in 2019 through 2020, had confidently stayed at a lowered cost, until it started to rise. Gasoline, an even more extreme incline, at 2020 rose rapidly towards a dark red, symbolizing a severely inflated price.

What do you wonder?
If all of the prices are going up, how long will it take for the economy to balance, and how will the rising prices affect our lives?

How does this relate to you and your community? 
With the rising prices, our community will continually struggle to keep matching the rising prices, especially with the high unemployment rates. One good aspect of all this, is that with the constant inflation of gasoline, it is pushing us to continue innovation with electric vehicles and healthier energy sources; cleaner energy is required to heal our planet from the pollution we have released and distributed in our atmosphere.

I notice that television prices have been on a steady decrease. Gasoline has somewhat been up and down, and recently has begun to increase once again. Used cars are beginning to increase once again, and sports equipment has begun to increase.

What to I wonder?
I wonder why. Some of this is somewhat unusual, like home furniture and sports equipment; why are these important enough to even include?

What impact does it have on you and your community?
Well, an increase in pricing effects everyone, generally. Most of these are goods being consumed by us, so the increase and decrease can either be helpful or unhelpful to the users.

A good title is, "Increasing and Decreasing Prices: Good or Bad?"
